title: The LLC Resonant Converter
subject: Power Electronics
blurb: Why half-bridge LLC exists, what the tank actually does, and how to read the gain curve without guessing.
prerequisites: AC circuit analysis in phasor form

slides.title:
The LLC Resonant
Converter
slides.lead: Why the topology exists, what the tank is really doing, and how to read the gain curve without guessing.

slides.title:
You cannot shrink the magnetics
without cooking the FETs
slides.lead: Every designer gets the same instruction: make it smaller. Smaller means higher switching frequency, because magnetic volume falls as frequency rises. That part works. What happens to the switches does not.

columns.label: Raise the frequency
items: Transformer core volume drops
Output filter shrinks
Faster transient response
Higher power density, smaller enclosure

columns.label: And you pay for it
items: Switching loss scales directly with frequency
Every turn-on dumps the energy stored in C<sub>oss</sub>
V and I overlap during the transition, heating the die
EMI gets worse at exactly the frequencies that matter

slides.callout: In a hard-switched converter, switching loss is roughly proportional to frequency. Double the frequency, double the loss. That is the wall — and resonant conversion is the attempt to walk through it.

slides.title:
Turn the switch on when its voltage
is already zero

points.text: Loss comes from overlap. If Vds has already fallen to zero before the gate rises, there is no overlap and no turn-on loss.
The tank must be inductive. Current has to lag the voltage so it keeps flowing after turn-off and discharges Coss.
The dead time has to be long enough. Drop the current or shorten the dead time and the discharge never finishes.

slides.callout: Drag the sliders. Whatever voltage is left on C<sub>oss</sub> at turn-on gets dissipated inside the die — this is how FETs die in a badly tuned resonant converter.

slides.title:
Half-bridge, three reactive elements,
transformer, rectifier

legend.role: Half-bridge at fixed 50% duty with dead time. Regulation comes from frequency, never duty.
Resonant capacitor. Also blocks DC, so the transformer never sees a DC bias.
Resonant inductor. Often just transformer leakage — which is why construction matters so much.
Magnetizing inductance, deliberately made small enough to take part in resonance.
Isolation and the turns ratio n that sets the nominal operating point.
Rectifier. Reflects the load back into the tank as an equivalent AC resistance.

slides.callout: Three reactive elements — two inductors and one capacitor — is where the name comes from: L, L, C.

slides.title: There are two resonant frequencies
slides.lead: Most explanations quote a single resonant frequency and then cannot explain the shape of the gain curve. The circuit has two, and the entire operating map lives between them.

formulas.label: Series resonance
formulas.note: Lm is shorted by the reflected load, so only Lr and Cr resonate. Here the tank is purely resistive and gain is 1 at any load. This is the design anchor.

formulas.label: Magnetizing resonance
formulas.note: When the secondary stops conducting, Lm is unclamped and joins the resonance. Because Lm is much larger than Lr, this sits well below fr. It is the lower bound of the boost region, not the ZVS boundary — that lives higher up.

points.text: Above fr the converter behaves like a series resonant circuit — gain is always below 1.
Between fm and fr the converter can boost above 1. This is the useful region.
Somewhere between them the tank turns capacitive and ZVS is lost. That crossover is not at fm — it depends on load, and it is the subject of slide 11.

slides.title:
Pretend the square wave
is a sine wave
slides.lead: The half-bridge produces a square wave, but the tank is a sharp filter centred near fr. It passes the fundamental and rejects almost everything else. So we analyse the fundamental alone and throw the harmonics away. This is the first harmonic approximation, and it is the reason LLC has closed-form design equations at all.

columns.label: What it buys you
items: The tank becomes an ordinary AC voltage divider
Phasor analysis applies — no time-domain simulation needed
One closed-form gain equation covers the whole design space
Accurate to a few percent near f<sub>r</sub>, which is where you operate

columns.label: Where it breaks
items: Well below f<sub>r</sub> the harmonics matter and the error grows
At very light load the secondary conducts discontinuously
It cannot predict the exact peak gain — always leave margin
It says nothing about the ZVS condition; check that separately

slides.callout: Use FHA to size the tank, then verify in simulation. Designers who trust the peak gain number without margin are the ones who find out at the low-line corner in production.

slides.title:
The whole converter collapses
into four components

points.text: The source becomes a sine at the switching frequency, amplitude 2Vin/π.
The rectifier and load collapse into one AC resistance, Rac = 8n²Rload/π². Heavy load means small Rac.
Lm sits in parallel with Rac. When the secondary conducts, Rac dominates and effectively shorts Lm out.

slides.callout: Everything from here on is this circuit. Read it as a voltage divider: the series Lr–Cr branch against the parallel Lm–Rac branch.

slides.title:
Sweep the frequency
and watch the divider work

points.text: Above fr the series branch is inductive and dominates. It drops most of the voltage, so gain falls below 1.
At fr Lr and Cr cancel exactly. The series branch vanishes, the full source appears across the load, and gain is 1.
Below fr the series branch turns capacitive while Lm starts to matter, and the divider begins to boost.

slides.callout: Drag fn first and leave the other two alone. The unity crossing at fn = 1 does not move — that is the whole reason fr is the design anchor.

slides.title:
Every load curve passes through
the same point
slides.widgetTitle: Interactive LLC gain curve — load sweep

points.text: Q is the load. Q = √(Lr/Cr)/Rac. High Q is heavy load, low Q is light load.
Heavy load flattens the curve. Peak gain collapses, so the worst case for boost is always full load at low line.
Light load peaks hard and the peak moves toward fm, which is why no-load regulation is awkward and needs burst mode.
All curves meet at fn = 1 with gain 1, regardless of Q. Load-independent by construction.

slides.callout: Now drag Q. Watch the peak collapse as the load gets heavier while the unity point stays nailed down.

slides.title:
m sets how much boost
you are allowed to have
slides.widgetTitle: Interactive LLC gain curve — m sweep

points.text: m = (Lr+Lm)/Lr. It fixes the gap between the two resonances: fm/fr = 1/√m.
Small m means a large Lr relative to Lm. Wide gain range, but high circulating current and poor efficiency.
Large m means a nearly conventional transformer. Efficient, but the curve flattens and there is barely any boost available.
Typical designs land between 3 and 8, chosen to just cover the required gain at the low-line, full-load corner.

slides.callout: This is the central trade of LLC design: gain range against efficiency. Every other choice follows from where you settle it.

slides.title:
Three regions, and only
one of them is home

points.text: Two boundaries, not two frequencies. fr is a fixed vertical line. The capacitive boundary is not — it is the curve joining the peaks of every load curve, so it moves with load.
Region 2 is the design target. Inductive tank, ZVS intact, gain above 1 when you need it.
Region 3 is acceptable. Still ZVS, but you are buying gain reduction with circulating current.
Region 1 destroys hardware. Not inefficient — destructive. The next slide is entirely about why.

slides.callout: Press Sweep and watch the marker cross the boundaries, or click a region to jump straight to it.

slides.title:
Past the peak the tank goes capacitive
and the FETs stop surviving
slides.lead: Region 1 is not a low-efficiency corner you can live with. It is a failure mode. Join the peaks of every load curve and you get the line that separates inductive from capacitive operation — cross it and the current leads the voltage, reversing the entire mechanism that made soft switching possible. Heavier load pushes that line to a higher frequency, so full load at low line is where you meet it first.

columns.label: The chain of events
items: Tank current leads voltage instead of lagging it
At turn-off there is no current left to discharge C<sub>oss</sub>
The body diode conducts, then is force-commutated off
Reverse recovery dumps a current spike through the die
Shoot-through, then the half-bridge is gone

columns.label: How you end up there
items: Startup, before the output has built up
Output short circuit — the controller chases gain downward
Overload at low line, pushing past the peak of the gain curve
A control loop with no hard low-frequency clamp

slides.callout: Note the shape of the trap: the controller lowers frequency to raise gain, but past the peak, lowering frequency lowers gain. The loop chases the wrong way and drives itself into region 1. Every practical LLC controller has a minimum frequency clamp for exactly this reason.

slides.title:
What the currents are
actually doing

points.text: iLr is close to sinusoidal because the tank rings at fr regardless of how fast you switch it.
iLm is a triangle. Lm sees the reflected output voltage clamped across it, so its current ramps linearly.
The secondary carries the difference. Where the two traces separate, the output diodes conduct; where they meet, the secondary goes dark.

slides.callout: Press Run. The magnetising current is the part that never reaches the load — it circulates, and it is the price of soft switching.

slides.title:
Circulating current is not waste,
it is the fee
slides.widgetTitle: Animated LLC waveform explorer — load sweep

points.text: iLm at turn-off is what discharges Coss. Remove it and you lose ZVS — this current is buying the soft transition.
But it flows through the FETs and windings anyway, producing conduction loss that delivers nothing to the output.
Smaller Lm means more of it, so more ZVS margin and worse efficiency. Larger Lm is the reverse.
Light load is the hard case. Drop the load slider and watch the useful current shrink while the circulating current stays put.

slides.callout: This is why m from slide 9 and the ZVS window from slide 2 are the same conversation. Choosing m is choosing how much you overpay for soft switching at every operating point.

slides.title:
Lm is fixed twice,
and the smaller number wins
slides.lead: The gain curve gives you one value of Lm through m. The dead time gives you a completely independent ceiling. Nothing guarantees they agree, and the deck so far has only shown you the first one.

formulas.label: From the gain requirement
formulas.note: m came from the boost you need at low line. This is the value that makes the gain curve reach.

formulas.label: From the ZVS requirement
formulas.note: The magnetising current has to swing the half-bridge node across the full bus inside the dead time. Larger Lm means less current to do it with.

points.text: Take the smaller. If the ZVS ceiling is below the gain value, you cannot have the m you wanted — raise fr, lengthen tdead, or pick a FET with less charge.

Co(tr) is not the Coss on the front page. It is the time-related equivalent, derived from the output charge Qoss integrated across the full Vds swing. Using the spot value at 400 V will flatter your design badly.
Worst case is light load at high line. Least magnetising current, largest swing to make. If ZVS holds there it holds everywhere.

slides.callout: Two FETs, a quarter of a resonant period, and the Coss of both devices are what produce the 16. Treat it as a sizing bound, not a precision result — it assumes the magnetising current stays flat through the transition, which it does not quite.

slides.title:
Three numbers, and every one
of them fights the others
slides.lead: Once the turns ratio is fixed, an LLC tank is fully described by f<sub>r</sub>, m and Q. There is no configuration that wins on all three axes — the design is choosing which compromise you can live with.

columns.label: Push it this way
items: Higher fr — smaller transformer and output cap
Smaller m — wide gain range, survives deep brownout
Lower Q — taller gain peak, easier to hit low line
Larger n — lower primary current for the same power

columns.label: And this is the bill
items: Higher fr — core and driver losses climb, layout gets unforgiving
Smaller m — more circulating current, worse full-load efficiency
Lower Q — Q is set by the load, not by you; it is a constraint, not a knob
Larger n — more gain demanded from the tank at low line

slides.callout: Q is the one people get wrong. You do not choose Q — the load chooses it. What you choose is Lr/Cr, and Q is what that ratio becomes at full load. Design at the worst case: full load, low line.

slides.title:
From a spec sheet
to Lr, Cr and Lm

points.text: Fix n so gain is 1 at the nominal bus. n = (Vin,nom/2) / Vout, which parks you at fr where the converter is happiest.
Find the gain you need at the low-line corner: M = nVout / (Vin,min/2).
Pick m and Q so the peak of the full-load curve clears that gain with margin. Never design to the peak — FHA overestimates it.
Solve the tank. Rac = 8n²Vout²/π²Pout, then Lr = QRac/2πfr, Cr = 1/2πfrQRac, Lm = (m−1)Lr.

slides.callout: Drag Vin min down and watch the required gain line rise until the curve can no longer reach it. That collision is the real boundary of your design.

slides.title:
What the equations
do not tell you
slides.lead: FHA gets you a tank that works at the nominal operating point. Everything below is what turns that tank into a product, and none of it falls out of the gain equation.

columns.label: Things that bite
items: Startup. Output is at zero, so demanded gain is enormous. Soft-start by sweeping frequency down from well above fr.
No-load regulation. The light-load curve peaks so hard that frequency control runs out of range. Burst mode is the usual answer.
Dead time versus Lm. Slide 14 gives the bound. What it does not give you is the dead time itself — too long and you lose conduction window and gain range, too short and ZVS collapses at light load.

columns.label: Things that surprise you
items: Leakage is part of Lr. Change the winding and you have changed the resonant frequency. Integrated magnetics make this a feature; discrete builds make it a tolerance problem.
Cr tolerance moves fr directly. Use film, not ceramic — class 2 ceramics lose capacitance under DC bias and temperature.
Short circuit is region 1. The loop chases gain downward into the capacitive region. A minimum frequency clamp is mandatory, not optional.

slides.callout: The single most common LLC failure in production is not a bad tank. It is a controller with no low-frequency clamp meeting a transient it was never simulated against.

slides.title: What you now know
slides.lead: Five ideas carry the entire topology. If these are solid, the datasheets and application notes will read like notes rather than mysteries.

formulas.label: The anchor
formulas.note: Gain is 1 here at every load. Design so the nominal input parks you on this point.

formulas.label: The shape
formulas.note: m sets the width of the boost region, and with it the trade between gain range and circulating loss.

points.text: Soft switching is the point. Everything in the topology exists so the FET turns on at zero volts.
Two resonances, three regions. Region 2 is home, region 3 is tolerable, region 1 destroys hardware.
Circulating current is the fee you pay for ZVS, and m is where you set the price.
